metadata.description: Learn ten bowel changes and other possible colon cancer warning signs worth discussing with a healthcare professional, plus risk factors and what a check may involve.
metadata.title: 10 Colon Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore

landing.title: 10 Colon Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore
landing.intro: Some bowel changes are easy to miss. See which 10 warning signs deserve attention.

disclaimer: General educational information only. These signs do not prove that someone has colon cancer and this guide is not a diagnosis or substitute for care from a qualified healthcare professional. Seek urgent medical advice for heavy bleeding, bloody diarrhoea, black or dark-red stool, severe worsening pain, persistent vomiting or signs of bowel obstruction.

sources.label: American Cancer Society signs and symptoms

sections.title: 10 Colon Cancer Warning Signs
sections.intro: Colon cancer may cause no symptoms at first. When symptoms do appear, they can have many non-cancerous causes, so a healthcare professional needs to assess the whole picture.

points.title: Blood in or on your stool
paragraphs: Blood may look bright red, dark red or make a stool appear unusually dark or black. Haemorrhoids and other common conditions can also cause bleeding, but visible or repeated blood should not be self-diagnosed.

points.title: Bleeding from the rectum
paragraphs: Bleeding noticed in the toilet or on paper is another change worth discussing. Seek urgent medical advice for heavy bleeding, bloody diarrhoea, or black or dark-red stool.

points.title: A persistent change in bowel habits
paragraphs: New diarrhoea, constipation, softer stool, or going more or less often than is normal for you can be significant when the pattern persists rather than settling quickly.

points.title: Stools that look narrower or different
paragraphs: A lasting change in stool shape or calibre can occur for several reasons. What matters is a noticeable change from your usual pattern, especially when it appears with bleeding, pain or weight loss.

points.title: Feeling that your bowel has not emptied
paragraphs: You may still feel an urge to have a bowel movement immediately after going. A repeated sensation of incomplete emptying deserves assessment if it is new or persistent.

points.title: Abdominal pain or cramping that does not settle
paragraphs: Ongoing stomach or abdominal aches, cramps, gas pains or discomfort can have many explanations. Pain that continues, worsens or occurs with other bowel changes should be checked.

points.title: Persistent bloating or fullness
paragraphs: Frequent bloating or a feeling of fullness may accompany changes in the bowel. A new pattern that does not resolve is more important than occasional bloating after food.

points.title: Unexplained tiredness or shortness of breath
paragraphs: Slow blood loss from the bowel can sometimes lead to iron-deficiency anaemia. This may cause unusual fatigue, weakness, breathlessness, dizziness or paleness and can be detected with a blood test.

points.title: Losing weight without trying
paragraphs: Unintended weight loss can have many medical causes. It should be discussed with a healthcare professional, particularly when it occurs with appetite loss, bowel changes, bleeding or persistent discomfort.

points.title: A lump or swelling in the abdomen
paragraphs: A new abdominal lump, swelling or persistent area of fullness needs medical assessment. Do not wait for a lump to become painful before seeking advice.

next.title: But Who Is Most At Risk?
next.copy: Symptoms are only part of the picture. Age, bowel conditions, polyps and family history can all affect underlying risk.

sections.title: Colon Cancer Risk: 10 Things Worth Knowing
sections.intro: Risk factors cannot predict who will develop colon cancer, and people without obvious risk factors can still be diagnosed. They can, however, affect screening and assessment decisions.

points.title: Getting older
paragraphs: Colon and colorectal cancer risk rises with age, although younger adults can also be affected. Screening recommendations vary by country, age and personal risk.

points.title: A previous colorectal polyp
paragraphs: Some types of polyps can become cancerous over time. A history of adenomatous polyps may mean that follow-up colonoscopies are recommended more often.

points.title: Previous colon or rectal cancer
paragraphs: People previously treated for colorectal cancer need an individual follow-up plan because they have a higher risk of another colorectal tumour.

points.title: A close family history
paragraphs: Risk can be higher when a parent, sibling or child has had colorectal cancer or certain polyps, particularly if diagnosis occurred at a younger age or several relatives are affected.

points.title: Inherited cancer syndromes
paragraphs: Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis are uncommon inherited conditions that substantially increase colorectal cancer risk and usually require specialist surveillance.

points.title: Long-standing inflammatory bowel disease
paragraphs: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease involving the colon can increase risk over time. This is different from irritable bowel syndrome, which does not cause the same inflammation.

points.title: Type 2 diabetes
paragraphs: Type 2 diabetes is associated with a higher risk of colorectal cancer. Individual risk still depends on many factors and should not be inferred from one condition alone.

points.title: Smoking and heavier alcohol use
paragraphs: Tobacco use and heavier alcohol consumption are linked with increased colorectal cancer risk as well as other health harms.

points.title: Weight, activity and diet patterns
paragraphs: Low physical activity, excess body weight, and diets high in processed or red meat are associated with greater risk. These are population-level associations, not a diagnosis for an individual.

points.title: Risk should guide a conversation
paragraphs: Tell a healthcare professional about relevant bowel disease, polyps and family cancer history. People at increased risk may need earlier or different testing than standard population screening.

next.eyebrow: KNOW THE SIGNS. KNOW THE RISK.
next.title: So How Do Doctors Actually Check For It?
next.copy: A symptom, stool test or blood result cannot diagnose colon cancer on its own. See how the investigation fits together.

sections.title: What Actually Happens During A Colon Cancer Check?
sections.intro: The pathway depends on symptoms, age, history and local guidance. These steps show a typical sequence, but not everyone needs every test.

points.title: Symptoms, medicines and family history
paragraphs: A clinician asks what changed, how long it has lasted, whether bleeding or weight loss is present, and what is normal for you. Previous polyps, inflammatory bowel disease, anaemia, medicines and cancers in close relatives can affect the next step.

points.title: Examination when appropriate
paragraphs: The abdomen may be checked for tenderness, swelling or a lump. Depending on the symptoms, a rectal examination may be discussed; the clinician should explain why and obtain consent.

points.title: FIT or another stool test
paragraphs: A faecal immunochemical test, called FIT, looks for small amounts of human blood in stool. It can guide referral and is also used in screening, but a positive result does not itself mean cancer and a negative result does not explain persistent symptoms.

points.title: Blood tests
paragraphs: A full blood count can identify anaemia and other tests can assess general health. Blood tests may add important context, but they cannot diagnose or rule out colon cancer by themselves.

points.title: Colonoscopy or another bowel examination
paragraphs: The NHS describes colonoscopy as the main specialist test for bowel cancer. A flexible camera examines the bowel lining; CT colonography or another investigation may be used in some circumstances.

points.title: Polyps, biopsy and imaging
paragraphs: Polyps may be removed and suspicious tissue sampled during colonoscopy. If cancer is confirmed in the laboratory, CT, MRI, PET or other tests may be used to assess its position, stage and relevant genetic features.

next.eyebrow: WHAT IF A TEST FINDS SOMETHING?
next.title: What Happens If Doctors Find Polyps Or Cancer?
next.copy: A polyp is not the same as cancer, and an abnormal test is not the end of the assessment. See how results lead to the next decision.

sections.title: What Happens If Doctors Find Polyps Or Cancer?
sections.intro: Results can range from a benign explanation to a polyp that needs surveillance or a confirmed cancer requiring staging. The sequence below separates those possibilities.

points.title: A FIT result shows blood
paragraphs: Blood detected by FIT can come from several causes. It usually creates a reason for further investigation rather than a diagnosis by itself.

points.title: A colonoscopy finds a polyp
paragraphs: Polyps are growths in the bowel lining and most are not cancer. Because some types can change over time, they may be removed and examined.

points.title: The polyp is removed where possible
paragraphs: Many polyps can be removed during colonoscopy. Their size, number, appearance and laboratory type help determine whether another colonoscopy is recommended later.

points.title: A biopsy is examined in the laboratory
paragraphs: Tissue analysis establishes whether cancer cells are present and provides information about the tumour. An appearance on camera or scan alone is not the final diagnosis.

points.title: Cancer is confirmed
paragraphs: A specialist team explains the result and coordinates further tests. A clinical nurse specialist may become a main contact for questions and support.

points.title: Scans and tests establish the stage
paragraphs: CT, MRI, PET, blood tests or genetic testing may be used depending on the site and circumstances. Staging describes how far the cancer has grown or spread and helps shape treatment.

points.title: A multidisciplinary team recommends treatment
paragraphs: Options can include surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy, alone or in combination. Tumour location, stage, genetic changes, age, health and personal preferences all matter.

next.eyebrow: ONE QUESTION PEOPLE OFTEN ASK NEXT
next.title: How Treatable Is Colon Cancer?
next.copy: The answer depends heavily on where the cancer is, whether it has spread and what the laboratory and scans show.

sections.title: Colon Cancer Outlook: What Really Matters
sections.intro: No single symptom or result can predict an individual's future. Doctors combine the stage, tumour biology, treatment response and overall health before discussing outlook.

points.title: Whether it is confined to the bowel
paragraphs: Cancer limited to the bowel is generally approached differently from disease that has reached distant organs. The exact depth of growth and nearby structures still matter.

points.title: Whether nearby lymph nodes contain cancer
paragraphs: Lymph-node findings help define stage and can influence whether treatment beyond surgery is recommended.

points.title: Whether it has spread elsewhere
paragraphs: The liver and lungs are among the sites doctors may assess. Advanced disease can still have treatment options, but the aims and combinations may differ.

points.title: Where the tumour is located
paragraphs: Cancers of the colon and rectum can require different surgical and radiotherapy approaches. The precise position also affects the practical treatment plan.

points.title: How the cells and genes behave
paragraphs: Laboratory features and certain genetic changes can help predict behaviour and whether targeted medicines or immunotherapy may be useful.

points.title: Whether all visible disease can be treated
paragraphs: Surgeons and other specialists assess whether the primary tumour and, in selected cases, spread to another site can be removed or treated effectively.

points.title: Response to treatment
paragraphs: Scans, blood tests and symptoms can show whether treatment is controlling the cancer. Plans may change as new information becomes available.

points.title: Age, health and personal priorities
paragraphs: Fitness, other conditions, recovery capacity and what matters most to the person affect which options are suitable—not merely age on its own.

points.title: Why earlier diagnosis can change options
paragraphs: Finding bowel cancer before it has spread can make treatment more straightforward, which is why persistent symptoms and screening invitations deserve attention.

points.title: Why statistics cannot predict one person
paragraphs: Survival figures describe groups treated in the past. They cannot account for every tumour feature, newer treatment or individual response, so the specialist team is the best source of personalised context.

conclusion.copy: Colon cancer can behave very differently from one person to another. Symptoms, FIT or one scan cannot determine an individual's outlook on their own; clinicians combine pathology, stage, health and response before discussing what happens next.
